subject: Chemistry
title: Count the Halogens: Mono, Di, Poly, Gem and Vic
summary: Halogen compounds are classified first by the number of halogen atoms: one is mono, two is di, three or more is poly (tri-, tetra-). Count the halogens, not the carbons: chloroform, CHCl₃, has one carbon but three chlorines, so it is a polyhalogen compound. Dihalides split by position: both halogens on the same carbon is a gem-dihalide (alkylidene halide, e.g. ethylidene chloride, 1,1-dichloroethane); on adjacent carbons a vic-dihalide (alkylene dihalide, e.g. ethylene dichloride, 1,2-dichloroethane).
keyPoints: **Count the halogens, not the carbons**: one X = **mono**, two = **di**, three or more = **poly** (tri-, tetra-).
**Same rule for haloarenes**: C₆H₅Cl is a monohaloarene, C₆H₄Cl₂ a dihaloarene.
**The CHCl₃ trap**: one carbon but three Cl, so chloroform is **trihalo**, a polyhalogen compound.
**Gem-dihalide**: both X on the **same carbon** (gemini = twins), e.g. CH₃CHCl₂; common name **alkylidene halide** (ethylidene chloride).
**Vic-dihalide**: X on **adjacent carbons** (vicinal = neighbour), e.g. ClCH₂CH₂Cl; common name **alkylene dihalide** (ethylene dichloride).
**IUPAC**: both are dihaloalkanes; locant **1,1 = gem**, **1,2 = vic**.
